articles.title: The Man Who Decided He Had Enough
articles.dek: A billionaire who secretly gave away his entire fortune helps unlock the most misquoted verse in the Bible — and the freedom hiding inside it.
articles.quote: It isn't money that wrecks a life — it's a grip on money that won't let go.
articles.body:
For fifteen years, nobody knew. The man behind one of the world's great fortunes flew economy class. He carried a ten-dollar watch and a plastic briefcase. He didn't own a house or a car. And while reporters chased other billionaires for interviews about their yachts, this one was quietly giving away almost every dollar he had — anonymously, through a foundation lawyers weren't allowed to name in public.

His name was Chuck Feeney. He co-founded Duty Free Shoppers, the airport retail chain, and became one of the richest men alive. Then he did something almost no one in his position does: he set out, on purpose, to die broke. His foundation's motto was "Giving While Living." By the time he passed away in 2023, he had given away roughly eight billion dollars — to universities, hospitals, human rights causes, peace efforts in Northern Ireland — and kept about two million for himself and his wife. When asked why, Feeney didn't philosophize. He just said, "I simply decided I had enough money."

That sentence is worth sitting with, because it's the exact crossroads Paul is standing at when he writes to a young pastor named Timothy in the city of Ephesus. Timothy was leading a church being pulled apart by false teachers — men Paul describes as conceited, obsessed with controversies, and treating godliness as "a means to financial gain" (1 Tim 6:5). They had figured out that religion, dressed up well, could be profitable. Paul doesn't argue with their logic. He exposes what's underneath it.

Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs. (1 Timothy 6:9–10, NIV)

Here's what's worth noticing: almost everyone quotes this verse wrong. You've probably heard it as "money is the root of all evil." Say it slowly and compare it to what Paul actually wrote. He doesn't say money is the root — he says the love of money is. And he doesn't say it's the root of all evil, as if every sin traces back to a dollar sign. He says it's a root of all kinds of evil — one tangled root among others, capable of producing a wide variety of ugly fruit, but not the sole explanation for human wrongdoing.

That distinction changes everything. Money itself is not the villain in this story. A wallet has no moral temperature. What Paul is diagnosing is a posture of the heart — a love, a craving, a grip that won't open. And that grip can close just as tightly around someone with very little as it can around someone with a fortune. The danger was never the coin. It was the clutching.

This is why Paul doesn't end with a warning. He ends with a picture of health. Just a few verses earlier, he writes, "godliness with contentment is great gain... if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that" (1 Tim 6:6, 8). Contentment isn't resignation — it's the thing that finally loosens the grip. And later in the chapter, Paul turns to address those who already have wealth directly, not to shame them, but to redirect them: "Command those who are rich in this present world not to be arrogant nor to put their hope in wealth... but to put their hope in God... Command them to do good, to be rich in good deeds, and to be generous and willing to share" (1 Tim 6:17–18). That's not a condemnation of having. It's an instruction on how to hold.

Chuck Feeney never read this as a theology lesson, as far as we know — but he lived it with startling precision. He didn't despise money; he built an empire with it. He simply refused to let it own him. Long before "effective giving" became a movement, before other billionaires publicly pledged their fortunes, Feeney had already quietly proven it could be done — and done without needing anyone to watch. He wasn't chasing applause. He was closing his hand on something else: what Paul calls, in the very next breath, "the life that is truly life" (1 Tim 6:19).

Most of us will never manage a fortune like his. But the test in this passage isn't about the size of your bank account — it's about the size of your grip. It shows up in smaller places: the overtime you pick up not because you need it but because you're afraid of not having enough, the comparison that creeps in while scrolling, the tight chest when giving is asked of you. The question Paul is really asking isn't "How much do you have?" It's "What has hold of you?"

So here's something worth trying this week, in Feeney's own quiet key: name your "enough." Not as a vague idea, but as an actual line — an amount, a lifestyle, a point past which more wouldn't make you freer, just heavier. Then let your hand open around something smaller than a fortune: an hour given away, a bill paid for someone else, a tithe that costs you something real. Paul calls this "storing up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the coming age" (1 Tim 6:19) — not because generosity earns heaven, but because an open hand is what a free heart looks like from the outside.

You don't need eight billion dollars to practice this. You just need to decide, like one tired but free old man once did, that you have enough.

articles.title: The Deed in the Clay Jar
articles.dek: While Babylon's army camped outside the walls and the city was starving, Jeremiah spent his last silver on a field he would probably never farm — and had the paperwork notarized to prove it.
articles.quote: Real hope isn't a feeling you wait to arrive. It's a transaction you're willing to make before it does.
articles.illustration: Lahaina taro fields replanted after 2023 fire
articles.body:
In August 2023, a wildfire tore through Lahaina, Maui, so fast that people had minutes, not hours, to get out. It killed more than a hundred people and flattened a town that had stood for two centuries. Everyone assumed the land itself was a loss — scorched earth, nothing left to salvage.

But when cultural practitioners walked the burned ground along the Kaua'ula stream months later, they found something nobody expected. The fire had stripped away a century of invasive grass and old sugarcane debris, and underneath it, the stone outlines of loʻi kalo appeared — ancient taro terraces that Hawaiian families had farmed for generations before they were buried and forgotten. Within weeks, farmers were back on that ash-covered ground, replanting taro in soil that was barely cool. The town wasn't rebuilt. The grief wasn't over. They planted anyway, because that's what you do with a field you still believe has a future, even wrapped in smoke.

Twenty-six centuries earlier, a prophet made a stranger bet in a city that was actually still burning. Jerusalem was under siege. Babylon's army had dug in outside the walls, and food inside the city was running out. King Zedekiah had thrown Jeremiah into the courtyard of the guard for the crime of telling the truth — that the city would fall, that the king would be captured, that there was no version of this where Jerusalem simply held on (Jer 32:1-5). It was, by any measure, the worst possible week to buy real estate.

That's exactly when Jeremiah's cousin Hanamel showed up with an offer. Under Israel's kinsman-redeemer law, family land couldn't pass to strangers — a close relative had first right to buy it and keep it in the family (see Leviticus 25:25). Hanamel's field sat in Anathoth, in territory the Babylonian army already controlled. It was, on paper, worthless. You couldn't farm it. You couldn't even safely visit it. And Jeremiah, sitting in prison with a death sentence hanging over the whole city, recognized the offer as "the word of the Lord" (Jer 32:8) and said yes.

What happens next is oddly, wonderfully specific. Jeremiah doesn't just agree in principle. He weighs out seventeen shekels of silver. He signs the deed. He seals it. He calls in witnesses to watch the whole transaction (Jer 32:9-10). Then he makes two copies — one sealed for the official record, one open for reference — and hands both to his assistant Baruch, in front of everyone sitting in that courtyard, with a very specific instruction: put these in a clay jar, so they'll last a long time (Jer 32:13-14). Jeremiah wasn't buying a field to farm it himself. He was filing paperwork for a future he almost certainly wouldn't live to see.

"For this is what the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel, says: Houses, fields and vineyards will again be bought in this land." (Jeremiah 32:15, NIV)

Here's what's easy to miss on a first read: Jeremiah had been preaching doom for decades. He wasn't an optimist by temperament — he's the prophet history nicknamed "the weeping prophet." He knew exactly how bad things were about to get, probably better than anyone else in Jerusalem. And it's precisely that man, sitting in a prison cell with the city collapsing around him, who spends his savings on land he can't use and has the deed sealed in a jar for safekeeping. Not because he felt hopeful. Because he'd been told something true about the future, and he decided to act on it in a way that would outlast him.

It's worth asking why he bothered with the clay jar at all. A verbal promise would have cost nothing. A private conviction in his own heart would have cost nothing. But Jeremiah made his hope auditable — witnessed, signed, sealed, buried for someone else to dig up later and confirm he meant it. That's a strange kind of faith: not a feeling you keep to yourself, but a record you leave behind for people who haven't been born yet.

Most of us never buy a literal field in a war zone. But we get smaller versions of Jeremiah's choice more often than we notice. It's the parent who keeps saving for a child's schooling during a month when the budget barely survives. It's the couple who keeps showing up to counseling for a marriage that hasn't shown a flicker of improvement yet. It's the friend who keeps calling, keeps forgiving, keeps investing in a relationship that every reasonable signal says is finished. None of that feels like hope in the moment. It usually just feels like stubbornness, or foolishness, or throwing good money after bad. Jeremiah's neighbors probably thought the same thing about him.

The difference between a feeling and a decision is that a decision survives the absence of the feeling. Jeremiah didn't need to feel hopeful to buy that field — he needed to believe God's word was true, and then act like it, with silver and signatures and witnesses who could hold him to it. That's a kind of wisdom that has nothing to do with optimism and everything to do with trust: you don't wait for the circumstances to justify your hope before you invest in it. You invest, and let the hope outlast the circumstances.

So here's something to carry today. Is there a field in your life right now that looks worthless — a relationship, a dream, a piece of ground you've written off because the siege outside looks permanent? You don't have to feel ready. You just have to be willing to sign for it. Make one small, concrete move that only makes sense if good things are still coming: the phone call you've been avoiding, the money you set aside anyway, the apology you offer before you're sure it'll be received. Seal it up, so to speak, and let time prove whether you meant it. Jeremiah never got to walk that field himself. But fields in Anathoth were bought and sold again within his grandchildren's lifetime — because somebody, decades earlier, had been willing to believe it first.

articles.title: The Cry He Could Pick Out of a Thousand
articles.dek: A quiet discovery about newborns and their mothers unlocks a strange, tender detail hiding inside one of the Psalms' most personal lines.
articles.quote: He turned his ear to you long before you called — which is why, like the psalmist, you can call on him as long as you live.
articles.body:
In the maternity ward, researchers once ran a quiet experiment. They gathered a room of new mothers, each only a day or two past delivery, and played them a recording: a string of infant cries, one after another, pulled from different babies on the same ward. No faces. No names. Just sound. Then they asked each mother one question: which cry is yours?

Most of them got it right. Not because they had memorized some unique pitch or rhythm their baby used — newborn cries are notoriously similar, more alike than different to an untrained ear, even to specialists who study them for a living. They got it right because somewhere in the space of a few feedings and a few sleepless hours, something in them had already tuned itself. A mother does not analyze her way to recognizing her child's cry. She simply turns her head before she knows why. Her ear has already decided. Researchers have found the same thing works in reverse: newborns only hours old, who have never seen their mother's face, will change the rhythm of their own sucking to trigger a recording of her voice over a stranger's — recognizing, through nine months of muffled sound in the womb, the one voice that was always theirs.

That image — an ear that turns, almost on its own, toward one voice out of many — sits at the center of one of the most tender lines in the whole book of Psalms.

The psalmist does not open with theology. He opens with a memory of drowning. "The cords of death entangled me, the anguish of the grave came over me; I was overcome by trouble and sorrow" (Psalm 116:3). Picture a man going under — not metaphorically wading through hard times, but pulled down, wrapped in something he cannot untangle, water closing over his head. He does not compose a prayer. He does not even manage a full sentence. Four words surface: "Lord, save me!" (Psalm 116:4).

That is the whole petition. No argument for why he deserves rescue. No eloquence. Just the cry of a man going under, the same way an infant's cry carries no vocabulary, no explanation, only need.

And here is what the psalmist says happened next:

I love the Lord, for he heard my voice; he heard my cry for mercy. Because he turned his ear to me, I will call on him as long as I live. (Psalm 116:1–2)

Notice the order. The psalm doesn't open "I love the Lord because he is worthy of love in the abstract," the way a creed might. It opens with something smaller and more personal: he heard my voice. The love comes after, as a response. This is a man who loves God the way you love someone who turned toward you when you called — not because you reasoned your way into it, but because you were heard, and being heard changed you.

Read it slowly, too, and a small, strange detail stands out. The psalmist doesn't simply say God heard him — he says God turned his ear to him. In the Hebrew, that word carries the sense of leaning, inclining, bending toward. It is not the language of a cosmic monitor passively receiving a signal among billions of others. It is the language of a mother in a nursery full of noise, turning her head before her mind has caught up, because something in her already belongs to that one voice.

It's worth asking why the psalmist reached for that image at all. He could have simply said, "God answers prayer." Instead he describes something closer to being singled out — found, the way a particular cry is found inside a room full of similar ones. The comfort isn't only that the Lord has good hearing. Omniscience, left on its own, can feel cold — a vast attention spread evenly over everything, the way sunlight falls on a field without noticing any one blade of grass. What the psalmist describes is warmer and stranger than that. He describes being distinguished.

Verse 6 makes the same point from another angle: "The Lord protects the simplehearted; when I in weakness was overcome, he saved me." The simplehearted — the word suggests someone without guile, without the polish to argue their own case, much like an infant who cannot explain what's wrong, who can only cry. The psalm does not say God protects the articulate, the composed, the ones who pray in complete sentences. He protects the simplehearted. The cry itself is enough, if it reaches an ear that has already turned toward you.

This changes something about how the moment of crisis — the entangling cords, the trouble and sorrow of verse 3 — actually functions in the psalm. It isn't only the danger. It's the occasion where the psalmist discovers, almost by accident, that he was already known. He didn't have to get God's attention from scratch, the way you'd flag down a stranger on the street. He found, in his drowning, an ear already bent toward him, the way a mother's ear is already bent toward her child before the first cry of the night ever sounds, and the way a newborn's whole body already knows the one voice worth turning toward.

There's a practical gentleness in this for anyone who has ever felt that their prayers were too plain, too repetitive, too unpolished to matter. We sometimes treat prayer like a performance that needs to earn a hearing — the right words, the right posture, enough faith measured out correctly, as if God were a switchboard operator rationing attention among too many calls. But the psalmist's whole testimony rests on four blunt words and a God who had, apparently, been listening for them all along. You do not need to compose something impressive. You do not need to clean up the cry before you bring it. You need only to let the real sound out, the way an infant does, trusting that the one who loves you has already tuned an ear in your direction, long before you learned how to speak in full sentences to him.

If you are carrying something tangled tonight — a diagnosis, a debt, a goodbye you didn't choose, a fear with no clean name — you do not need to find the right words for it first. Say the plain thing. "Lord, save me" is a complete prayer. It was enough for the psalmist, entangled and overcome, and it is enough now. You are not required to explain yourself to the one who already turned toward you before you opened your mouth.

And when the answer comes — not always instantly, but it comes — let it do what it did for him. Not just relief, but recognition: he heard my voice; he heard my cry for mercy. Something in you may have believed you were one voice among billions, easily lost in the noise of a world this loud. The psalm insists otherwise. A mother can find her own child's cry in a room full of strangers' children. So can your Father. He turned his ear to you long before you called — which is why, like the psalmist, you can call on him as long as you live.

articles.title: The Hand That Wouldn't Feed Itself
articles.dek: Kodak invented the camera that could have saved it and sat on the patent for twenty years. Proverbs 19 says laziness often looks less like doing nothing, and more like almost finishing.
articles.quote: God is patient with slow hands, but he is not interested in a faith that stops at the edge of the bowl.
articles.body:
In 1975, a twenty-four-year-old engineer named Steven Sasson carried a strange, toaster-sized box into a conference room at Eastman Kodak. He had built it in a back lab out of spare parts and borrowed components, and it did something no device in history had ever done: it captured a picture without film. It took twenty-three seconds to record a grainy black-and-white image onto a cassette tape, and the only way to see the photo was to play the tape back through a television. It was clunky. It was slow. But it worked. Sasson demonstrated it to a room of Kodak executives, the very people whose company had built an empire on film and paper and chemicals. One of them reportedly smiled, impressed, and then said the sentence that would echo through business schools for the next fifty years: "That's cute. But don't tell anyone about it."

Kodak didn't destroy the invention. They patented it. They kept it. They just never brought it fully to their lips. For almost two more decades, the company that had invented the digital camera sat on the digital camera, afraid that eating this new meal would spoil the one they already had on the table. By the time Kodak finally tried to swallow what had been sitting in their hand all along, the rest of the world had already built the feast without them. The company that once owned ninety percent of the film market in America filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

It is, strangely enough, almost exactly the picture Solomon paints in Proverbs 19. He is not talking about cameras or corporations. He is talking about a man at dinner. Picture it slowly, because it is almost comic if it were not so sad. The food is not far away. It is not locked up, rationed, or hidden from him. His own hand is already in the bowl. His fingers are already wet with the meal. All that remains is the shortest, easiest motion in the world -- lifting a loaded hand the last few inches to his own mouth -- and somehow, he cannot finish it.

"A sluggard buries his hand in the dish; he will not even bring it back to his mouth!" (Proverbs 19:24, NIV)

Older translations call this man merely lazy, and that is true as far as it goes. But notice what the proverb actually describes. This is not a man who refuses to reach for the dish at all. He has already done the hard part. He has already reached in. His failure comes at the very last step, the step that should have been easiest, the step of finishing what he started. That is worth sitting with, because most of us are not tempted to do nothing at all. We are tempted to almost finish. We read the book and never apply the chapter. We feel the conviction and never change the habit. We hear the apology forming in our chest and never let it reach our mouth. Like the sluggard, our hand is already in the dish. The distance left to travel is almost nothing. And still, so often, nothing moves.

Kodak's own engineers kept pointing this out internally for years. They had the data. They had the warnings. They had their own invention staring back at them every time they opened the patent file. Solomon has a word for that kind of refusal too, a few verses later in the same chapter: "Stop listening to instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge" (Proverbs 19:27). It is one thing to lack knowledge. It is another thing entirely to have the instruction sitting right there, already in your hand, and simply decide not to let it travel the last few inches into your life.

But Proverbs 19 does not leave us with only a warning. Just one verse before the sluggard, it offers the opposite picture, the one worth aiming for: "Rebuke the discerning, and they will gain knowledge" (Proverbs 19:25). Notice the gentleness of what is required here. The fool needs a flogging to learn anything at all -- that is the sobering half of the verse. But the discerning person needs only a quiet word, a correction, a nudge, and they let it do its full work. They do not just hear it and nod. They carry it all the way through. The difference between the fool and the wise is rarely the size of the warning they receive. It is almost always whether they let the warning finish its journey.

This is where the gospel steps into Solomon's dinner scene and does something wonderfully practical. On the night before he died, Jesus took bread, broke it, and said, "Take and eat; this is my body" (Matthew 26:26). He did not simply set the bread on the table and explain its meaning from a distance. He put it directly into the disciples' hands and told them to finish the motion -- to take it all the way to their mouths, to receive it, not merely to admire it. Grace, like that bread, is not useful to us sitting in the dish. It has to be received. God is patient with slow hands, but he is not interested in a faith that stops at the edge of the bowl. He asks us to actually eat -- to let forgiveness travel from the page into the apology, to let conviction travel from the sermon into the changed habit, to let his mercy travel from a comforting idea into an actual, lived change of life.

So it is worth asking honestly where your own hand might already be sitting in the dish. Perhaps it is a conversation you know you need to have, and you have rehearsed every word of it a hundred times in your head but never once out loud. Perhaps it is a grudge you already know, in your most honest moments, God wants you to release -- you have even prayed about it -- but you have not yet said the words of forgiveness to the person's face, or even to yourself. Perhaps it is a Bible reading plan, a budget, a doctor's appointment, a long-overdue phone call to a parent. The hard part, the reaching in, may already be behind you. What remains is the smallest, most ordinary motion: lifting what is already in your grip the rest of the way home.

Kodak's story did not have to end the way it did. The company had everything -- the patent, the prototype, the twenty-year head start -- except the willingness to let what was in its hand reach its mouth. Solomon's sluggard did not need more food. He needed to finish an inch of motion he had already begun. And most of us, if we are honest, are not waiting on God for some new provision today. We are only waiting on ourselves to finish lifting what he has already placed, generously and specifically, into our open hand.

Whatever that last inch is for you this week, take heart: it is shorter than it feels, and it is the only step left between you and the feast already in your grip.
